title: Protest and Comments of Constellation Energy Generation, LLC in response to PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s 02/23/2026 60-Day Compliance Filing under ER26-1479.

UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                           BEFORE THE
                             FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.                                            )                 Docket No. ER26-1479-000

    PROTEST AND COMMENTS OF CONSTELLATION ENERGY GENERATION, LLC

           Constellation1 protests limited provisions in PJM’s Sixty-Day Compliance Filing2 that are

non-compliant with the Commission’s December 18, 2025 Order3 because they fail “to make the

directed changes.”4 First, the replacement of “Point of Interconnection” in the definition of Co-

Located Load with “Point of Change in Ownership” contradicts the Commission’s order. Second,

the proposed Behind the Meter Generation (“BTMG”) rules expand BTMG to include a 50-MW

threshold and thus create a large class of favored resources at the expense of Co-Located Load.

Constellation also seeks clarification of PJM’s filing in several other areas to ensure compliance,

to accelerate the interconnection of large loads, and to prevent undue discrimination against Co-

Located Load and the generators seeking to serve it.

                                                     PROTEST

           In two important areas, PJM’s proposal is outside the scope of compliance, falls short of

the Commission’s intent, and perpetuates existing undue discrimination that has delayed the

interconnection of large loads for years.



1
    Constellation Energy Generation, LLC (“Constellation”) files this protest pursuant to Rule 211 of the Commission’s
    Rules of Practice and Procedure. 18 C.F.R. § 385.211 (2025).
2
    PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Sixty-Day Compliance Filing for Co-Located Load Related Revisions to Open Access
    Transmission Tariff to Comply with Commission Order in Docket No. EL25-49-000, et al., Docket No. ER26-1479-

3

4

    filings must be limited to the specific directives ordered by the Commission. The purpose of a compliance filing is
    to make the directed changes and the Commission’s focus in reviewing them is whether or not they comply with the
    Commission’s previously-stated directives.”); see also Cal. Power Exch. Corp., 101 FERC ¶ 61,330, at P 25 (2002)
    (“The purpose of a compliance filing is to make only the revisions directed by the Commission.”).
      I.    The Commission Should Reject PJM’s New Definition of Co-Located Load as Outside
           the Scope of Compliance, or in the Alternative, Require Further Modification

           As with PJM’s Thirty-Day Compliance Filing,5 the Commission should reject PJM’s

proposal to use its Sixty-Day Compliance Filing to replace the Commission-mandated “Point of

Interconnection” in the definition of Co-Located Load with the “Point of Change in Ownership.”6

Changing the specific definition of Co-Located Load already approved by the Commission is

outside the scope of compliance. The December 18th Order adopted the following definition of

Co-Located Load: “a ‘configuration [that] refers to end-use customer load that is physically

connected to the facilities of an existing or planned Customer Facility on the Interconnection

Customer’s side of the Point of Interconnection to the PJM Transmission System.’”7 The

Commission neither sought comment on nor directed PJM to propose a new definition of Co-

Located Load. Nor did the December 18th Order permit PJM to propose variations that PJM

considered were “consistent with or superior to” the Commission’s adopted definition as the

Commission does with amendments to the pro forma Generator Interconnection Agreements.8

 Consistent with the Federal Power Act and longstanding Commission precedent, if PJM “wished

to depart from or challenge” the Commission’s adoption of PJM’s definition of Co-Located Load,

it “should have filed for rehearing” of the December 18th Order.9 PJM did not do so. In fact, PJM

had multiple opportunities to express concerns with the Commission “adopt[ing] PJM’s

definition.”10 The Commission should “not allow [PJM] to pursue such matters on compliance”

and should reject PJM’s departure from the Order.11

            Subsequent discussions between PJM and Constellation have not resolved Constellation’s

concerns regarding PJM’s definition.12 The “Point of Change in Ownership” definition will not

“afford[] greater certainty to all interconnection parties.”13 PJM overlooks the record evidence of

discrimination by Transmission Owners against Co-Located Load that does not connect directly

with the Transmission Owner. Using the “Point of Change in Ownership” could give the

Transmission Owner an additional tool to discriminate against competing projects.14 Unlike the

Interconnection Facility18 instead of a Project Developer Interconnection Facility. The

Transmission Owner could assert that the equipment and load both fall on the Transmission

Owner’s side of the Point of Change in Ownership and no longer qualify as Co-Located Load.

Below is an illustration of a hypothetical example to demonstrate this point. Even if such claims

might eventually be overturned by the Commission, changing the definition of Co-Located Load

would allow Transmission Owners to use the determination of the Point of Change in Ownership

to cause unnecessary delay or other mischief for large load projects seeking speed to service from

competitive suppliers.

            Constellation’s example of a new ring bus configuration added to accommodate a large

load, included in its Thirty-Day Compliance Filing Comments, illustrates the difference, as shown

above.19 A ring bus allows the load to access supply from the generation facility and the grid.

Using the “Point of Interconnection” to define Co-Located Load allows any load connected on the

ring bus to be included as Co-Located Load—even if the Transmission Owner owns some or all

of the new facilities on the ring bus. By contrast, using “Point of Change in Ownership” to define

Co-Located Load could allow a Transmission Owner that owns some or all of the new facilities to

assert the ring bus is not a Project Developer Interconnection Facility, thereby preventing the load

from qualifying as a Co-Located Load at all.

           PJM’s justification for using the Point of Change in Ownership misses the mark because it

ignores the fact that new facilities will need to be added to tie in the new large loads and that

generators do not have sole control over the configuration of these facilities and instead are subject

to Transmission Owner and PJM interconnection specifications, with any attempt to dispute

Transmission Owner requirements resulting in an interconnection delay.

           Indicated Transmission Owners argue that Constellation’s concerns are “unsubstantiated”

and “speculative.”20 This is incorrect. Significant record evidence shows that the Transmission

Owners have engaged in discriminatory conduct to frustrate Co-Located Load configurations.21

This includes, as the Indicated Transmission Owners acknowledge,22 letters sent by a PJM

Transmission Owner stating it will resume work to allow Co-Located Load arrangements only if

interconnection process to continue to deny, delay, encumber, or tie interconnection services for

large load configurations that they disfavor. Alternatively, if the Commission accepts PJM’s

 II.        The Commission Should Reject PJM’s 50-MW Materiality Threshold for BTMG, or in

PJM’s existing BTMG rules” the Commission “decline[d]” to address Constellation’s argument

“that charging all Eligible Customers taking transmission service on behalf of large Co-Located

Loads for NITS based on a gross demand basis would be unduly discriminatory because it is

eligibility for future BTMG to a 50-MW threshold and thus substantially adds to the ability to

            PJM’s 50-MW materiality threshold for BTMG is 150 percent larger than the 20-MW

threshold suggested by the Commission based on the definition of a Small Generator and

400 percent larger than the 10-MW threshold it suggested based on PJM’s requirement for

individual generator metering.30 This broadly expands the availability of new special behind-the-

meter generation arrangements that will be constructed, or will have sufficient backup

generation,31 to fall under the 50-MW threshold to take advantage of netting, reduce their

transmission costs and otherwise receive preferential treatment over Co-Located Load. Combined

with PJM’s proposed legacy treatment,32 the exceptions allowing for netting will swallow the rule

against it. A vast swath of new PJM generators and loads would be allowed to follow the precise

BTMG rules that the Commission deemed “unjust and unreasonable.”33

            Under PJM’s proposed 50-MW threshold, a significant number of loads with BTMG would

be able to take advantage of netting and include backup generation as offsetting BTMG. Such

             PJM also states that a 50-MW threshold would “avoid unneeded regulatory uncertainty for

retail customers whose grid impacts on reliability are more limited”40 and “small or de minimis.”41

Fifty MWs of power could serve a large town or small city.42 PJM provides no support for this

claim. In addition, PJM argues that “many of the existing Retail BTMG are decades old and may

need significant upgrades prior to directly interconnecting into the PJM system,” but “given the

costs associated with such significant upgrades, the owners of such resources may decide to forgo

the option of interconnecting into the PJM system altogether.”43 PJM again provides no support.

Nor does PJM explain how exempting load backed by capacity presumably unsuitable for

interconnection furthers the Commission’s goal of “reduc[ing] the reliability and resource

adequacy risks that large or increasing BTMG may pose to PJM.”44

            PJM’s 50-MW materiality threshold is unsupported and does not address Constellation’s

undue discrimination arguments. The Commission should reject the threshold and direct further

compliance or require alternative modifications to address undue discrimination.

appropriate to ensure compliance with the December 18th Order.

      I.     The Commission Should Require PJM to Clarify the Necessary Studies Process for
            Project Developers to Ensure Speed to Market

            To achieve speed to market, we recommend three clarifications to PJM’s proposed

Necessary Studies Tariff language: (1) clarify the scope of the Necessary Studies analysis to ensure

Project Developers are able provide the required information for PJM to timely complete its

reviews; (2) clarify Project Developers with existing Necessary Studies for Co-Located Load

arrangements do not have to restart the Necessary Studies process and be further delayed; and

(3) establish deadlines to complete the Necessary Studies process expeditiously and accelerate the

interconnection of Co-Located Loads.45

                    A. Additional Clarification on the Scope of the Necessary Studies Process Is
                       Needed

            Additional clarity is needed regarding the scope of the Necessary Studies to be performed

by PJM to ensure that Project Developers are able to provide the models and other information

required for PJM to timely complete the Necessary Studies process.46 PJM proposes to define the

scope of the Necessary Studies to “include thermal, short circuit, and stability studies under various

seasonal and load conditions, as specified in more detail in the PJM Manuals.”47 It is not clear

whether PJM is proposing to use the existing Necessary Studies process or a new process. In

addition, the Necessary Study Agreement requirements set forth in PJM Manual 14C do not

specifically reference the studies to be performed. To achieve the Commission’s goal of
